cu.auto.lead: Add this service to your Project's compose file, alongside the nzbfast service, and it checks nightly at 04:00 for a newer image. Set the timezone to yours.
cu.auto.unraid: On Unraid you do not need any of this: Community Applications adds an Auto Update Applications page under Settings that can keep nzbfast current on its own.
cu.copied: Copied. Paste it into your compose file.

cu.intro: nzbfast is running in a container, so it never replaces its own files: you move it forward by pulling a newer image. Your settings, queue and downloads live in the folders you mounted, and survive the swap.
cu.now.click: If you created it by searching the Registry and clicking Run: Registry → re-download the latest tag, then Container → stop nzbfast → Action → Reset.
cu.now.p2: Build (this pulls the new image), then Start.
cu.now.project: If you created it as a Project (Container Manager or Portainer):
cu.now.unraid: If you installed it on Unraid from Community Applications: Docker tab → Check for Updates at the bottom of the page, then click the nzbfast icon and choose Apply Update. Your ports, paths and settings are kept.
cu.pinned: One thing that catches people out: none of this moves a container that was created from a version tag such as :1.0.3. Both Watchtower and a manual re-pull fetch the tag the container was created with, so use :latest if you want updates to arrive.
cu.socket: Worth knowing before you paste it: this needs the Docker socket, and mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives that container root-equivalent control of the machine. If you would rather not, skip it and have your NAS run docker compose pull && docker compose up -d on a schedule instead. On Synology that is Control Panel → Task Scheduler → Create → Scheduled Task → User-defined script, run as root.
cu.stuck: If it does not come back after updating, the container prints why it stopped and the reason is in its own log: Container Manager, then Container, nzbfast, Details, and the Log tab. Over SSH that is docker logs nzbfast. Nothing is lost while it is stopped, and deleting the container or your config folder will not help.

role.arr.blurb: Downloads arrive over the API and the results are handed to something else. These four make that handover behave the way those apps expect.
role.arr.dupe: Failing a duplicate straight into History is what Sonarr and Radarr expect: it lets them pick a different release themselves instead of waiting on a copy that is being held for them.
role.arr.giveup: After three different releases of the same episode have all failed, the item is unmonitored instead of a fourth dead copy being fetched.
role.arr.index: The built-in index feeds the wall, which is a browsing surface an app-driven install never opens. Switching it off stops the scanning and the disk it uses.
role.arr.umask: Finished files are left group-readable, so an app running as a different user in the same group can import them. Without it a systemd install keeps everything owner-only and the import silently finds nothing.
role.hint: Each answer is a short list of recommendations with the reason for each one. Nothing changes until you press Apply, and every row is an ordinary setting you can change back on its own afterwards.
role.import.hint: Scans this machine for the configuration, shows you what it found, and asks before writing anything.
role.link.watch: Watch folder, post-processing script and passwords file
role.nzbget.blurb: The same one button: nzbfast reads the nzbget.conf already on this machine and brings over the servers, the categories and their folders, and the passwords file. Post-processing scripts keep working - they are given the NZBPP_, NZBOP_ and NZBPR_ variables and the 93/94/95 exit codes they expect, and a comma-separated list of them runs in order.
role.sab.blurb: The move itself is one button: nzbfast reads the configuration already on this machine and brings over the servers, the categories and their folders, and the passwords file. Nothing you have here is replaced - servers already present are skipped.
role.solo.blurb: Nothing needs changing - this is what a fresh install already does. The one thing worth switching on is the part of it that is off by default.
role.solo.index: Indexing the groups you choose fills a browsable wall of posters, the way a media library does, and it is what the watchlist matches against. Nothing is scanned until you pick what to index.

rule.warn.literal: This did not compile as a pattern, so it is being searched for as plain text - which usually means the rule never matches anything.
rule.warn.not.all: This "but not" matches every release, so the rule is switched off.
rule.warn.not.literal: This "but not" did not compile, so it is being searched for as plain text and will almost never match.
sb.badsrc: the account picked as the reference is no longer in your indexer list, or is turned off there. Pick another one.
sb.cal.done: "have" is partly an estimate from size and timing. Spot-checked {n} times so far, and the guess was right {ok} times ({pct}%).
sb.cal.none: "have" is partly an estimate from size and timing, and nothing has measured that guess yet. The spot-check switch above puts an error bar on it.
sb.cooling: asked to slow down; next try after {time}
sb.idxoff: the indexer is off, so there is nothing to measure.
sb.noidx: enter a reference indexer address and your API key first: the sample is drawn from your own account.
sb.perday.cal: plus up to {n} downloads for the spot-check

sel.pause.title: Pause the selected downloads

set.adv.title: Essential hides the advanced settings in every section; nothing is lost and the count tells you what is hidden
set.alt.autosearch: Look for a replacement when none is held
set.alt.autosearch.hint: off unless you turn it on. Searching spends new traffic on a release you did not pick, so this one asks first by default. Never done for a download Sonarr or Radarr sent: they blocklist and re-search themselves, and two of you hunting one episode gets it grabbed twice
set.alt.autoswitch: Switch to a held copy without asking
set.alt.autoswitch.hint: when a download turns out to be one that cannot finish, start the best copy already being held for it instead of putting a button on the queue row. It spends no more than the download you already asked for, because the release is the one you chose and the backup .nzb is already on disk
set.alt.hold.hint: when a download is grabbed from a search, keep this many of the next-best matches ready as backups. Only the small .nzb files are kept - a few kilobytes each - and nothing is downloaded from them unless a copy is switched to. 0 keeps none; 2 or 3 is plenty
set.alt.maxbytes.hint: a ceiling on what switching copies may add on top of the download you asked for: e.g. 20G, or 0 for no limit. 0 is the right answer on an unmetered account and the wrong one on a block account, where every byte of a second copy is paid for
set.alt.maxcopies.hint: how many copies of one release this may spend in total, the first attempt included. Stops a title nobody can supply from being tried all night
set.cardlink.manual: Could not reach the clipboard - the link is in the address bar now.
set.cardlink.title: Copy a link straight to this section
set.cats.base.title: what happens when a download in this category finishes
set.cats.match.title: matched against the release name, case-insensitive
set.cats.name.title: shown on the wall tabs and cards
set.cats.none: no custom categories: everything files under Movies, TV, Apps or Other
set.cats.offered: your apps are offered this category as "{slug}"
set.cats.offered.none: type a name and this is the short name your apps will be offered
set.cats.remove.title: Delete this category
set.cats.rules.hint2: give sport, wrestling, podcasts, audiobooks or anything else its own wall category. Each release name runs through these top to bottom, first match wins, ahead of the built-in Movies/TV classifier. Match rules are regexes or wildcards like *anime* (plain keywords work too), same as Smart folder rules. "Treat as" decides what happens when a download finishes: movie-like and TV-like get junk cleanup and renaming; "leave as posted" touches nothing, which is the safe choice for books, comics and audio. Each one is offered to your apps as well, under the short name at the end of its row - add that name to the list above to give it a folder of its own
set.cats.title: Your categories
set.chk.auto: Check finished folders on a schedule
set.chk.auto.bytes.hint: a ceiling on what one check may spend on repairs, e.g. 20G. 0 does not mean unlimited here: it means nothing is repaired automatically, and there is no value that takes the ceiling off. Each repair is counted against this at the full size of the download it repairs, not at the size of the damaged part, even though a repair usually fetches far less than that. Counting it the pessimistic way is the point: a ceiling that holds in the worst case holds in every case. For a folder that was unpacked from an archive the worst case is the ordinary case, because none of what is on the disk can be reused
set.chk.auto.every.hint: weekly by default, because a check costs a full read of the folders it reaches and files do not go bad by the hour. 1 to 8760, which is a year. A new value applies from the next check onwards. The first check of a session runs a quarter of an hour after nzbfast starts, and the clock is not remembered across restarts, so a machine restarted more often than this checks more often than this; what bounds the cost of that is the two limits below, not this number
set.chk.auto.hint: off unless you turn it on. Every so often nzbfast goes through the finished folders that have a check file, checks each one against it, and starts a repair for whatever no longer matches, without anybody clicking. It never runs while a download is running or waiting, and it steps aside as soon as one arrives. Checking is not free: it reads every file in a folder from end to end, unpacked films included, so a library where nothing is wrong still costs the disk that read. At most 200 folders are looked at each time, and the next round carries on where the last one stopped, so a big library is covered over several rounds instead of one enormous read. Two things it will not do on its own: repair a download that is no longer on record here, because finding another copy of it means a search and what comes back may not be what is on your disk; and touch a download whose size it does not know, because then it cannot count what the repair would cost. Both are still offered by the Check it button above, where you can look at them first. Needs the check file setting at the top of this card: a folder without one cannot be checked
set.chk.auto.jobs: Most repairs to start each time
set.chk.auto.jobs.hint: how many damaged downloads one check may start repairing. Four by default, and 16 at the very most, which is the same limit the Check it button above has: that button tells you the whole count before you press it, and this one tells nobody anything, so it is kept well below it. Damage past the limit is not forgotten, it waits for the next check or for the button above. 0 finds the damage and repairs none of it
set.chk.cap: {n} downloads are started at a time. Check the folder again afterwards to start the rest.
set.chk.clean: Everything in that folder still matches what the download proved.
set.chk.dir.hint: reads every file in the folder and compares it with what the download proved. It reports what no longer matches and offers to repair it, and on its own it downloads nothing - repairing is a second, separate click. Only folders that have a check file in them can be checked
set.chk.dir.ph: the folder a finished download went into
set.chk.foot: Repairing fetches only the damaged part. Everything in the folder that is still intact is read straight off the disk, so a single bad file does not cost you the whole download again.
set.chk.head.many: {n} files in that folder no longer match what the download proved.
set.chk.head.one: {n} file in that folder no longer matches what the download proved.
set.chk.keep: Keep a check file in each finished folder
set.chk.keep.hint: every download proves a checksum for each file it fetched, and then throws it away: the .par2 files that carried it are cleaned up, so months later there is nothing left to check the folder against. With this on, those checksums are kept in a small hidden file called .nzbfast.manifest beside the payload, and a folder can be checked, and repaired, years after it was downloaded. It costs no extra downloading, and one quick read of the finished files as the download ends. Turn it off and finished folders get no such file; a folder that finished while it was off cannot be checked later, because there is nothing to check it against
set.chk.rest: {n} were not started this time. Check the folder again to start them.
set.chk.src.none: That download is no longer on record here, and the name is not one a search can be aimed with, so this cannot be repaired.
set.chk.src.recorded: The download it came from is still on record here, so nothing has to be searched for.
set.chk.src.search: That download is no longer on record here, so another copy of it would be searched for by name.
set.chk.started.many: {n} repairs are on the queue now.
set.chk.started.one: {n} repair is on the queue now.
set.chk.title: Checking downloads later
set.chk.unident: These no longer match either, and cannot be repaired: the check file does not record which download they came from.
set.db.cap.hint: how big the index is allowed to get, e.g. 20G. Empty or 0 = no limit. On its own this deletes nothing: the switch below is what acts on it
set.db.evict: Delete releases to stay under it
set.db.evict.hint: off unless you turn it on. With it on, releases are deleted as the index grows past the limit, in the order below; they come back only if a later scan finds them again
set.db.evictnow.hint: run one pass immediately instead of waiting for the index to reach the limit
set.db.headroom.hint: how far below the limit a cleanup empties, so the very next scan does not trigger another one. 10 means it deletes down to 90% of the limit; 0 stops exactly at it
set.db.kinds.hint: clear a box to protect that kind: those releases are never deleted to save space. Everything ticked = anything can go
set.db.lag: Deleting releases frees space inside the database file, but the file itself only gets smaller once it is compacted, and a compact waits for a moment when nothing is downloading or scanning. So the size above can sit still for a while after a cleanup. The size limit is measured against what is actually stored, not against the space waiting to be reclaimed.
set.db.order.hint: the default ladder spends the least useful entries first, so a full index loses dead fragments long before it loses anything you would search for
set.db.order.ladder: junk and incomplete posts, then oldest, then largest
set.db.preview.hint: counts what a cleanup would delete - to the size in the Shrink box below if you typed one, otherwise to the size limit - and deletes nothing
set.db.pv.head.many: A cleanup to {size} would delete about {n} releases ({bytes} of index data).
set.db.pv.head.one: A cleanup to {size} would delete about {n} release ({bytes} of index data).
set.db.pv.more: It stopped counting there: a real cleanup would delete more than this.
set.db.pv.none: Nothing would be deleted: the index is already under {size}.
set.db.pv.short: Even deleting all of that would not reach that size.
set.db.scope.all: no: anything can go, in the order above
set.db.scope.hint: limits what a cleanup may touch at all. With a scope set, a limit the allowed rows cannot satisfy stops short and says so, rather than reaching into real releases
set.db.scope.incomplete: only incomplete posts may be deleted
set.db.scope.junk: strictest: only junk posts may be deleted
set.db.scope.junkinc: yes: only junk and incomplete posts may be deleted
set.db.shrink.hint: a one-off: delete releases until the index fits the size you type. It does not change the size limit above, and like the limit it leaves the file to be compacted once nothing is downloading or scanning
set.db.stat.compact: Last compacted {when}, returning {freed} to the disk.
set.db.stat.compact0: Last compacted {when}; there was nothing to reclaim.
set.db.stat.evicted.many: The size limit has removed {n} releases so far, freeing {size}.
set.db.stat.evicted.one: The size limit has removed {n} release so far, freeing {size}.
set.db.stat.free: {free} of that is already free inside the file: it drops to about {live} once a compact rewrites it.
set.db.stat.nevercompact: It has not been compacted yet; that happens at an idle moment.
set.db.stat.over: This is over the size limit.
set.db.title: Database
set.disk.cats.builtin.title: always available, so it cannot be renamed or removed - its folder is still yours to set
set.disk.cats.dir.ph: a subfolder of the download root
set.disk.cats.dir.title: where this category lands. Blank = its own subfolder of the download root; a plain name = that subfolder instead; a full path = downloads land in the root as usual and finished jobs move there
set.disk.cats.groups.title: pick this category for downloads added without one: comma-separated keywords or regexes matched against the NZB's own category tag and its newsgroups, e.g. alt.binaries.teevee. An NZB whose category tag equals this name matches with nothing here
set.disk.cats.hint: the categories offered to Sonarr, Radarr and other clients, and where each one's finished downloads go. tv, movies, music and books are always available; add any others your apps are set to use - a client whose category is missing here refuses to connect. Leave a folder blank and that category lands in its own subfolder of the download root, which is what most setups want. Rows are listed alphabetically, and a category an app sends that is not here yet adds itself
set.disk.cats.name.title: the name Sonarr, Radarr or your app is configured with
set.disk.cats.nzbname.title: name finished downloads in this category after their .nzb file. "default" follows the switch in Auto-rename & cleanup, so a category is how you allow or disallow it for one kind of download
set.disk.cats.prio.title: default priority for downloads added in this category; an add that names its own priority wins
set.disk.cats.remove.title: Delete this category
set.disk.cats.script.title: post-processing script for this category, instead of the global one (several, comma-separated, run in that order); blank = the global script
set.disk.cats.warn.comma: A folder cannot contain a comma or a semicolon - those separate the list.
set.disk.cats.warn.slash: A category is one folder name, so this will be saved as "{safe}".
set.disk.cats.wt.title: download straight into the full path on the left instead of moving there when the job finishes. Only does anything for a full path - a plain subfolder name is already on the download drive. Leave it off if that path is a network share
set.disk.minfree.hint: pause new jobs below this, e.g. 25G. Defaults to 2G so the disk never fills completely; 0 = off
set.disk.move.hint: after unpack and renaming, finished downloads move here - a NAS share, media drive etc. Category subfolders are kept. Empty = leave them in the download folder. If the destination is unreachable the files stay put
set.disk.nestdepth.hint: how many archive-in-archive layers to unpack automatically (default 5); applies to the next download. At the limit the deepest archive is left in place, unpacked no further - the download still completes. Raise only for unusually deep nested releases
set.disk.out.hint: completed downloads root (per-category subfolders) · applies to the next download; jobs already queued keep their destination · created automatically if it doesn't exist
set.disk.outperm.hint: a umask, the same number Docker and the setup guides use: 002 gives folders 775 and files 664, 022 gives 755 and 644. Leave it empty and nzbfast changes nothing, which is what it has always done. Set it when Sonarr or Radarr run as a different user in the same group and cannot read or import what lands here - on a systemd install they usually cannot, because the unit keeps everything the daemon writes owner-only to protect the API key. Ignored on Windows, which has no such thing
set.disk.pace.hint: how moves to the completed folder share the machine with downloads. "Yield to downloads" slows the move while anything is downloading and goes full speed when the queue is idle. Pick a speed to give moves a fixed share of the line, alongside the download speed limit. "Full speed" never slows the move - for setups where the two paths don't share a bottleneck
set.disk.quota.hint: byte budget per period, e.g. 500G; 0 = off. Force-priority jobs bypass it
set.disk.slowpause: Pause when the disk cannot keep up
set.disk.slowpause.hint: a drive that has started to fail often still accepts writes - it just takes minutes over them. The download then crawls, the graph sawtooths, and it all looks like a network problem. With this on, several minutes of stalled writes pause the queue with the reason and the folder named, keeping everything downloaded so far, and downloads start again by themselves once the drive answers normally. A brief busy spell never triggers it
set.disk.title: Disk & quota
set.disk.wt.hint: write files into the destination above from the start, instead of downloading here and moving them at the end. On a setup where the destination is a different drive, that turns every finished job from a full copy-and-delete into nothing at all, and no job ever needs room on two drives at once. Leave it off for a destination on a network share: every write then goes over the network for the whole download, rather than one bulk copy at the end. The unfinished download, its resume record and the repair scratch all live on the destination while it runs. Per-category ticks in Categories & folders below turn it on for one kind of download without turning it on for the rest
set.giveup.instances: Sonarr and Radarr it may act on
set.giveup.instances.hint: unmonitoring happens inside your Sonarr or Radarr, so each one needs its URL and API key here (in the *arr: Settings, General). The on box pauses an instance without forgetting its stored key; removing the row forgets the key too. Watchlist items need no entry - the watchlist is handled by nzbfast itself
set.giveup.name.title: label for the log line
set.giveup.none: no instances: only watchlist items can be given up
set.giveup.on.title: off pauses this instance without forgetting its stored key
set.giveup.remove.title: Forget this instance and its stored key
set.giveup.threshold: Give up after this many failed releases
set.giveup.threshold.hint: 0 = off, the default. When this many different releases have all finally failed for the same episode or movie, stop chasing it: the item is unmonitored in the Sonarr or Radarr that sent it (and the watchlist stops picking new copies of it), instead of downloading yet another dead copy. Below the threshold nothing changes - a failed grab is blocklisted and searched again as normal. A finished download for the item clears its count
set.giveup.title: Give up on dead content
set.hist.age.hint: age counted from the moment the download finished; 0 = this rule is off. It removes completed downloads only: a failed one stays until you retry it or delete it yourself, because it is a decision you have not made yet. Checked once a minute, so a short setting takes effect within about a minute of the entry ageing past it. Works alongside the limit below, not instead of it.
set.hist.age.title: how long a finished download stays in History
set.hist.age.unit.title: the unit the number beside this is counted in
set.hist.auto.hint: off = History keeps everything, which is what nzbfast has always done. Switch it on and the two rules below decide what goes. Only the History entry is removed - the downloaded files stay exactly where they are, and a job still finishing or still being moved is never touched.
set.hist.count: Keep at most this many entries
set.hist.count.hint: once History is longer than this the oldest entries go, whatever their outcome - unlike the age rule above, this one counts failed downloads too, because a length limit that could be filled with failures would stop being a limit. 0 = this rule is off. Works alongside the age rule, not instead of it.
set.hist.title: History cleanup
set.idx.adult.hint: on by default. Titles filed as adult are left out of the wall and the release list, whether the name came from a header scan or a spot. This is not the same control as the "Include adult" tick on the Browse page: that one only opens up the raw Spots list there, and it does not change what the wall shows
set.idx.backfill.hint: headers to fetch on a group's first scan
set.idx.can: What it finds: posts that were uploaded under a real filename. The scan reads newsgroup headers, so something posted as Some.Film.2026.1080p.WEB-DL.x264-GROUP.part01.rar is recognised, filed under its title, and shown on the wall with a poster, cast and ratings.
set.idx.cant: What it cannot find: posts with the name taken out. A large and growing share of Usenet is uploaded deliberately obfuscated: the subject is random (p5cbKvaDJ1Y0PW6DvKCIfztzZ), the filenames inside are random too, and it all goes into a catch-all group like alt.binaries.boneless. The real name exists only in an NZB the uploader publishes somewhere else, so it was never posted to Usenet at all and there is nothing on the wire for any scanner to read. This is not a gap we can close later: no competitor recovers those by scanning either.
set.idx.ccf.hint: off unless you turn it on. Even a strong suggestion from the matching above is still a guess from size and timing. This takes up to 24 of those guesses a day, searches the suggested name on an indexer account you already added, and fetches the matching NZB from it. The name is applied only when the message ids inside that NZB point at the very post held here, and it is then marked as proven; anything less leaves the suggestion for you to review. Each check spends one search and at most one download from that account's daily allowance, and nothing is sent anywhere else
set.idx.ccfsrc.hint: pick one of the indexer accounts you already added; its saved address, key and daily limits are reused. There is no box for a different account here on purpose: these checks download NZB files, which indexers count against an account, so only an account whose limits are already tracked can be asked
set.idx.ccfstat.hint: how much of today's allowance is used. What the checks settle shows in the counters above: a confirmed check moves a suggestion to confirmed, a miss leaves it alone, and a day with no strong suggestions spends nothing
set.idx.compact.hint: reclaim disk space freed by retention pruning (rewrites the database file). Runs only when no download or scan is active
set.idx.corr.hint: the public announcement channels carry no filenames, so most obfuscated posts cannot be matched directly. What an announcement does pin down is when a release appeared and how big it is. This compares announcement timing and size against unnamed posts and, when they fit, suggests the real name on the Browse page. A suggestion is clearly marked, needs your click to apply, and never renames files on disk.
set.idx.corrauto.hint: a match this needs is strict: the size must agree tightly, no other announcement may fit nearly as well, and the announcement must pick this post back when checked the other way around. Applied names change only how a release is shown, they are marked as inferred, and a finished download that proves one wrong takes it back off on its own. Everything weaker stays a suggestion for you to review.
set.idx.coverage.hint: scan new posts on each of your provider networks, not just one. Posts do not always reach every provider, and providers carry different newsgroups; scanning them all means a release stops looking incomplete when a different provider has the missing parts. The deepest provider still does the history work, the others only follow new posts. Prepaid block accounts are never used for scanning
set.idx.db.browse.title: Browse for the index database file
set.idx.deepen.hint: every scan pass also indexes this many OLDER articles per group, growing history in the background until Max age (or the group's start) is reached; 0 = off
set.idx.dropdb.hint: the database is kept while the indexer is off, so turning it back on picks up where it stopped instead of rescanning. Delete it if you want the disk space back now
set.idx.enabled.hint: off unless you turn it on. It scans the newsgroups you choose, straight from your provider, so you can search and browse Usenet here without a third-party account. Read what it does and does not find below before you decide.
set.idx.enrichpause.hint: stop fetching titles, posters and cast from the metadata sites. What has already been fetched stays; rows found from now on simply keep the name they were posted under until you turn this back off. The index itself carries on scanning - this is the only setting here that touches no news provider at all
set.idx.fold.hint: some uploaders post every piece of an upload under a different random poster name and spread the pieces across several groups, so one upload arrives looking like thousands of unrelated fragments. On each scan pass this spends a moment merging fragments that clearly belong together back into one entry. Merging only makes the entry whole, so its size and timing become real; it never guesses a name
set.idx.gapfill.hint: each scan pass picks this many incomplete releases and asks the other providers for headers around their posting time, filling gaps the scanning provider never received; 0 = off
set.idx.gates.hint: optional JSON filter on what gets indexed: kinds/years/resolutions/languages/title patterns/size, e.g. {"kinds":["tv"],"res":["1080p"],"min_size":"200M"}. Empty = index everything
set.idx.good: Worth turning on if you follow particular newsgroups where people still post under real names, you want to see what your provider actually carries rather than what somebody else says it carries, you want to judge retention and completeness yourself, or you would simply rather not depend on anyone else's service.
set.idx.groups.hint: comma-separated, e.g. alt.binaries.teevee; feeds Browse, the wall and the newznab facade
set.idx.iscdesc.hint: most providers send no descriptions at all, which leaves the group search matching names only. This fetches about 45,000 of them from ISC, a public Usenet directory. It is the only request nzbfast makes to anywhere other than your news provider, so it is off unless you turn it on.
set.idx.leftover: An index from earlier scanning is still on disk: {size}, {n} releases. It is not being read or added to.
set.idx.maxage.hint: only index posts newer than this; 0 = no limit. Keeps the database small
set.idx.noleftover: Nothing is stored: this indexer has never run here.
set.idx.nzbimport.budget.hint: most posted NZB files cost a single article; a large one is capped at about 48. The default 300 keeps up with the typical daily flow of these posts; 0 = off
set.idx.nzbimport.hint: some uploaders post the NZB file for a release next to the release itself. This fetches those small posted files and uses the message-ids inside them to confirm or recover the real name of an obfuscated post; prepaid block accounts are never used
set.idx.offdoes: With the switch off nothing is scanned, no headers are fetched, no metadata or artwork is looked up, and no availability sampling runs. The poster wall, Browse and the Sonarr/Radarr feed are hidden until you turn it back on. The watchlist stays as long as you have indexer accounts, because it can ask those instead.
set.idx.omdb.hint: optional: richer movie metadata on the wall (exact matches, cast, posters, IMDb ids) and ~4× faster movie enrichment. Free tier is 1,000 lookups/day. Empty = fully keyless
set.idx.omdbget.hint: only needs an email address: we submit the signup for you; OMDb emails you the key with an activation link. Or do it yourself at omdbapi.com/apikey.aspx
set.idx.par.hint: how many newsgroups one scan pass reads in parallel. Each takes connections from the same provider account your downloads use, so more is faster only up to the point where they start competing. 1 to 8; default 3
set.idx.pausedl.hint: stop indexing entirely while a download is running. Scanning takes NNTP connections from the same account (up to 15 of 20 at the default parallelism) and its database writes compete with the download for CPU and disk. Off = keep indexing during downloads, so new posts stay visible sooner
set.idx.pesto: Read names from tiny PAR2 posts
set.idx.pesto.budget.hint: each checked post costs a few small articles (well under 1 MB). The default 120 keeps up with the typical daily flow of these posts; 0 = off
set.idx.pesto.hint: one widely used posting tool uploads fully obfuscated posts and then posts their real name inside a small PAR2 file right after the data. This fetches that small file and only accepts the name when its hashes match the post it points to, so the wall can show what the post really is. A near miss is dropped rather than guessed; prepaid block accounts are never used
set.idx.pesto.state.hint: these posts all come from one posting tool, so the daily numbers here are the early warning: if named falls to zero or PAR2 files stop parsing, that tool changed something and this source is drying up
set.idx.predb.hint: off unless you turn it on. Plenty of uploads are posted with the name taken out, so a scan has nothing to read. Public relay channels announce the real name next to the filename a release was posted under, which is the one open way to match the two up. Turning this on keeps a connection open to an IRC network and listens. Nothing is ever posted, no account is created, and releases named this way are marked as having been named from the feed rather than read off the post.
set.idx.predbch.hint: comma-separated. Only what the channels announce is read; nothing is sent to them
set.idx.predbnick.hint: the nickname nzbfast uses on the relay. A few random characters are added to it so two installations never collide. Letters, digits and a little punctuation, up to 12 characters; anything else is dropped, and an empty box falls back to nzbfast. Takes effect the next time the feed connects
set.idx.predbrows.hint: how many announced names the table holds; past that, the oldest are dropped. Only names posted after an announcement can be matched by it, so keeping more only helps if you are also matching older posts. 10,000 to 5,000,000, default 250,000; a number outside that range is pulled back to the nearest end rather than refused
set.idx.predbseed.hint: the oldest announcement the import below will keep, in days. It is a limit rather than a target: the import reads only the newest couple of pages of each section, so in practice it stops well short of this. 1 to 366; default 180
set.idx.predbsrv.hint: the IRC network carrying the relay channels, as host or host:port
set.idx.predbstat.hint: a feed that quietly stops working looks exactly like one with nothing to say, so it reports both
set.idx.prefq.hint: when one film or episode has been posted several times, releases matching these float to the top of its list and get a “best match” mark. Nothing is ever hidden: release names leave tags out all the time, so this only changes the order. Leave any of them on “no preference” to ignore that one
set.idx.probe7z.budget.hint: each peeked post costs a few articles (about 1-2 MB). The default 150 keeps up with the typical daily flow of these posts; 0 = off
set.idx.probe7z.hint: many obfuscated posts carry their real name inside the posted archive itself. This peeks at two or three articles of each such post and reads the name from the 7z index, so the wall can show what the post really is. Works on unencrypted single-archive 7z posts; prepaid block accounts are never used
set.idx.probe7z.state.hint: nearly all of these posts currently come from a single uploader, so the daily numbers here are the early warning: if they fall to zero or locked headers appear, that uploader changed something and this source is drying up
set.idx.retention.hint: also delete already-stored wall-visible releases once they age past the max-age window, so the index holds ~that window instead of growing forever. Off = only gate new posts. Dead junk fragments (already hidden, still incomplete after a week) are always reaped regardless of this setting
set.idx.sb.hint: off unless you turn it on. Once a day this asks an indexer you already have an account with for its newest releases, then scores our own index against the answer: do we have each post, do we show the same name, and how far behind were we. The table below is the result. One small request a day for each category you tick below, on your own account, and nothing is ever sent anywhere else
set.idx.sbcal.hint: a post uploaded with its name taken out can only be matched by size and timing, which is a guess. This checks up to 5 of those guesses exactly each day by fetching their NZBs from the reference, which spends up to 5 of that account's daily downloads. The result is the error bar under the table. Off unless you can spare the downloads
set.idx.sbcats.hint: one request a day per ticked category, so untick the ones you do not care about to spend less of your indexer's daily allowance. Anything unticked is simply not measured - the table says so, and reads nothing into the silence
set.idx.sbkey.hint: your key from that indexer's account page. It is stored, never shown again, and only ever sent to the indexer it belongs to
set.idx.sbsrc.hint: pick one of the indexer accounts you already added, and its saved address and key are reused - nothing to type twice, and a new key entered there carries over here. Or choose to enter a different account below, for a reference you do not otherwise search
set.idx.sbstat.hint: what the last daily sample did. A run that hit trouble says so here rather than pretending nothing happened
set.idx.sburl.hint: the base address of the indexer to measure against, like https://api.example.org. Address only: anything with a ? in it is refused, so a pasted key can never ride along into a log. The key has its own box below
set.idx.scale: For scale, in our own measurements a full index of 14.8 million scanned posts yielded about 31,000 browsable releases. Roughly one in five hundred.
set.idx.scannow.hint: run a scan pass immediately; with a depth, one-off deep backfill: rescan that many recent headers per group even where already scanned (e.g. 500000)
set.idx.seed.hint: the live feed only hears announcements from the moment it is switched on. This fetches recent announcements from a public pre database, once, so posts that are already indexed can be matched too. Runs in the background for a few minutes; progress shows here.
set.idx.seed.terms: announcements come from predb.net, a public pre database run on one small server. Its operator asks people not to build their own database out of it, so this takes only the two newest pages of each section, at most 10 requests a minute, and stops. Running it again brings back the same announcements rather than older ones.
set.idx.slog.hint: on by default. Counts the searches made here and through the Sonarr/Radarr feed so the list below can say what people asked for and did not get. One row per distinct query, not a log of every keystroke. It stays on this machine, is never looked up anywhere and is never sent anywhere. Turning it off also forgets everything already recorded
set.idx.slogclear.hint: empties the list above and leaves the recording switched on
set.idx.slogstat.hint: what was asked for and not answered, most asked first. This is the list to work from when deciding which groups to scan or how far back to backfill. A query that stops appearing here is a gap the scanner has filled. Nothing acts on it by itself
set.idx.tip.hint: a short loop that reads only what is new at the head of each group, so a fresh post shows up in seconds instead of waiting behind the history work of the next full scan. When nothing has arrived it costs one command per group. Seconds; 0 turns it off and leaves the scan interval as the only path. Anything above 0 is held to at least 5. Default 20
set.idx.title: Indexing
set.idx.tmdb.hint: optional: uses TMDB for wall titles, posters and cast, and gives "Work out what a hidden film is" its second source. Empty is the normal setup and nothing is lost - metadata still comes from TVmaze and Wikidata, with no key at all. TMDB does not grant API access to Usenet tools, so this is for a key you already hold. Stored here and never shown again; a key already in your config file or TMDB_API_KEY still works and this box wins over both
set.idx.wallmeta.hint: clear every cached title/poster and re-download fresh; indexed releases are untouched
set.idx.want.hint: nothing is indexed unless you pick something here. Each choice scans the newsgroups listed under it, and only the ones your provider carries.
set.idx.why: Why a commercial indexer is still recommended: an indexer is told what a release is by whoever uploaded it, so it can name the obfuscated posts that no scanner can. It also carries years of back catalogue, and it is what Sonarr and Radarr expect. Add your accounts under Search indexers just above: searches on the wall can then ask them and grab straight into the queue, with none of this switched on.
set.idx.wipe.hint: delete the whole index database (releases, titles, artwork) and rescan from scratch: the fix for db corruption
set.ins.cap.hint: Nothing on Usenet stays up forever, so an item you queue paused for later can be half gone by the time you start it. Give this a budget and nzbfast quietly fetches those items' files now, while the posts are still whole, then unpacks one only when you start it. The number is how much disk that may use, in GB; 0 turns it off, which is what it does today. It runs only while nothing else is downloading and steps aside within seconds when a real download arrives, and nothing is ever deleted to make room - at the budget, nothing new is picked up
set.ins.title: Save paused downloads while you can
set.ins.wl.hint: New episodes and films the watchlist finds are queued paused instead of downloading straight away, so you decide when each one runs. With a budget above, their files are still fetched in the background while the post is whole, so waiting costs you nothing
set.lib.cats.hint: comma-separated; jobs in these become metadata-only .strm entries, downloaded on first play
set.lib.recheck.hint: how often parked library entries are re-verified (min 60)
set.lib.title: Library
set.look.accent.hint: used for links, buttons and the first chart series
set.look.accent.warn: hard to read on this background
set.look.allpass: Every pair clears the readable minimum.
set.look.border.hint: how visible the line around each card and control is. Strong helps if the edges are hard to make out
set.look.check.hint: measured against the WCAG 2.1 minimum of 4.5:1 for body text
set.look.colours.hint: override the theme's background, card and text colours. The readability check below measures whatever you pick, so you can see immediately if a pair stops being legible
set.look.corners.hint: how rounded cards, buttons and panels are
set.look.density.hint: how much room each card gets. Compact fits every figure in a small window; spacious gives them air
set.look.fill.hint: Dense preset only. Lets the dashboard drop to fewer, wider columns when that leaves less empty space under short cards; the page itself can come out a little taller. You can also stack a card by hand: right-click its heading and choose Stack under
set.look.font.hint: the more readable option picks the clearest faces already installed on this machine (wider letterforms, looser spacing); nothing is downloaded
set.look.motion.hint: charts glide and views fade in. Follows your system's reduce-motion setting unless you choose here
set.look.palette.hint: the series colours on every graph. The colour-blind-safe set stays distinguishable with deuteranopia or protanopia, which a red/green pair does not
set.look.preset.hint: Classic is a plain, light, compact dashboard with just the queue and history - the graphs and extra cards are hidden. Full brings the default back: auto theme, regular spacing, everything shown. Dense keeps everything but shrinks it - small cards several to a row, short graphs, made for big screens. Each simply sets the controls on this page and the dashboard cards, so any part can be adjusted afterwards; stored in this browser
set.look.reset.hint: puts the appearance and your card layout back to defaults. Your servers, folders, watchlists and every other setting are untouched: this card is stored in this browser only
set.look.share.hint: everything on this card, plus your card layout, as a file you can keep or load into another browser
set.look.somefail: Some text on this setting falls below the readable minimum. Pick a different accent, or switch theme.
set.look.theme.hint: Auto follows your system's light or dark setting
set.look.title: Appearance
set.nnab.list.hint: your accounts on NZB indexers (NZBGeek, DrunkenSlug, a Prowlarr or NZBHydra instance, …). Searches on the wall can then ask them too and grab results straight into the queue. API keys never leave this machine. The daily limits mirror your account's allowance: 0 means unlimited.
set.nnab.nzbi: Set the first box of a row to nzbindex to search nzbindex.com directly instead, with no account needed. It indexes what was actually posted rather than a curated release list, so it finds things an indexer will not - and many of its results carry scrambled names.
set.nnab.title: Search indexers
set.notify.body.ph: webhook body, e.g. {"content":"{name} finished"} - empty sends our own JSON. Placeholders: {name} {status} {category} {dir} {bytes} {error} {id}
set.notify.body.ph.text: message text, e.g. {name} is {status} - empty sends a stock line. Placeholders: {name} {status} {category} {dir} {bytes} {error} {id}
set.notify.events.ph: events: completed, failed, repaired, disk, quota - empty = finished downloads (plus fails, if ticked)
set.notify.events.title: route this target onto specific events. Leave empty for the classic behavior: every finished download, plus failures when the box is ticked. Naming events replaces both: only what is listed fires. repaired = a finished download that needed repair; disk / quota = the matching guard pausing the queue
set.notify.fail.title: also send when a download fails - useful for a chat webhook, noise for a library scan
set.notify.h.authhint: the token was rejected; check it below
set.notify.h.never: nothing sent to this target yet
set.notify.name.title: label for the log line
set.notify.none: no targets: nothing is notified when a download finishes
set.notify.remove.title: Stop notifying this target
set.notify.secret.ph: signing secret: requests carry X-NzbFast-Signature (HMAC-SHA256) when set
set.notify.secret.title: optional shared secret. Every request to this webhook then carries X-NzbFast-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of the body>, so the receiver can verify the sender. Blank keeps the stored secret
set.notify.targets.hint: Kodi, Plex and Jellyfin/Emby get a library rescan; a webhook gets whatever you write, so Discord, ntfy, Gotify and Home Assistant all work. Token = the Plex token, the Jellyfin/Emby API key, or user:password for a Kodi with a password set. Category limits a target to one category; empty = every download. Test sends one now
set.notify.title: Notifications
set.notify.tok.ntfy: access token (if the topic needs one)
set.perf.conns.hint: sockets PER SERVER for a download (each server's own account limit also applies); use Connection tuning on the dashboard to find the sweet spot
set.perf.fastpar.hint: speeds up repair of badly damaged downloads. Turns itself off automatically if a repair does not verify
set.perf.finalcheck.hint: the check that reads your finished files back from the disk, at the end of a download and when you run nzbfast verify by hand. Normally each file is proved by one digest over the whole file, and that is a single read on one core however many cores the machine has. With this on, each file is proved from the PAR2 set's per-block checksums instead, which run on every core at once. Much faster on a fast local disk, and worth very little on a network share or a spinning disk, where the disk is already the limit. What it costs: a PAR2 set can carry two records that describe different files, and other tools call such a set damaged where this calls it clean. No normal set is built that way, and a repair still proves itself the old way whatever this says
set.perf.fleet.hint: nzbfast normally chooses this for itself and grows it when a measurement says the line needs more: a small fleet finishes sooner than a large one on most lines, and asking for too many sockets is measurably slower. Leave it empty for that. A number fixes the whole fleet at that many connections, shared out across your servers and still inside each account's own limit above. 0 turns the rule off, so every server dials its own number. Worth setting only if "Why is this slow?" on a download says the connection budget is what is holding it back
set.perf.mem.hint: pipeline RAM cap, e.g. 8G; 0 = automatic (sized from this machine's RAM)
set.perf.title: Connections & performance
set.perf.verifymode.hint: how much of a download is checked as it arrives. Full confirms every PAR2 block with MD5. Fast claims blocks by CRC32 instead, 2-3× quicker on slow CPUs, and still checks every article's own CRC. Lean also skips those article CRCs once PAR2 covers a file, so damage is caught a moment later, at its block. Whichever you pick, the settle pass at the end and any repair use full MD5, and a download with no PAR2 files keeps article CRCs
set.perf.verifymode.lean: lean: CRC32 blocks, no article CRCs
set.remote.body: Point your phone's camera at a code, or type the address - same Wi-Fi works immediately. For access from anywhere, the painless answer is Tailscale (free, no router changes): install it on this machine and your phone, and a "works from anywhere" code appears above automatically. Remote-control apps work too: add nzbfast as a SABnzbd server (this address + your API key) or an NZBGet server (any username, API key as the password). Avoid raw port-forwarding - the dashboard is plain HTTP; if you must, always set an API key.
set.remote.here.hint: what to type into a browser on this machine, and what to bookmark there. Other machines on your network want one of the addresses below instead.
set.remote.opennote: No API key is set: anyone on your network can control nzbfast at these addresses. Set one in Security below.
set.remote.title: Remote access
set.rename.eg.eptitle: and an episode carries its own title:
set.rename.eg.event: and an event keeps its own words:
set.rename.eg.off: Off: files keep their original names
set.rename.eptitles.hint: name an episode file "Show - S01E02 - The Ceremony [1080p].mkv" instead of "Show - S01E02 [1080p].mkv". Off by default, because it changes filenames your library and your *arr apps have already matched on. The title comes from the episode list already stored for shows on your watchlist, so it never waits on the internet and never renames a file later: a show we have no list for keeps today's name. Titles are in the show's original language, usually English
set.rename.extrawords: Keep the other words in the name
set.rename.extrawords.hint: sport, races and other events are often one title repeated all season, and only a word or two apart: "Round11 Hungary Race" vs "Round11 Hungary Qualifying". Keeping those words is what stops them all becoming the same name. Only applies where the name could not be tidied up otherwise, so ordinary films are untouched
set.rename.fromnzb.hint2: the finished folder and its main file take the name of the .nzb file, instead of the tidied-up name worked out from the release. Only the biggest file is renamed: the rest of an episode pack, the sample, the subtitles and the .nfo keep the names they arrived with. Off by default, and any category can turn it on or off on its own under Categories
set.rename.identify: Work out what a hidden film is
set.rename.identify.hint: some posts arrive with the name stripped off them, so the video lands as a string of random characters. When that happens, read the film's own running time, picture and sound formats and subtitle languages, then look those up in public film databases. Films only, and only once the download has finished. It renames the file ONLY when two separate databases agree on exactly one film, which needs a TMDB key in the Indexing settings - without one it never renames, it just writes what it found into History so you can see what the file probably is
set.rename.identity: Ask public databases what a finished download is
set.rename.identity.hint: when a job finishes, look the release up in two free public databases (srrdb and xREL) to recover the name it was posted under. At most one request to each per download, no account and no key, and a failure is silent. On by default. Off means names come only from what is inside the files, which is what a post with its name stripped off does not have
set.rename.junk.hint: delete leftover .par2, .nzb, .sfv, .nfo and sample clips from finished movie/TV folders, never the video or its subtitles
set.rename.mediaonly.hint: ⚠ permanently deletes everything except the video(s) and subtitles; every episode of a season pack is kept
set.rename.on.hint: give the folder and main file a clean, informative name: a movie becomes "Example Movie 2024"; TV keeps "Show - S01E02". Obfuscated or unrecognized names are left exactly as posted
set.rename.qbrackets.hint: "… [1080p x265]" instead of "… 1080p x265". Off by default
set.rename.title: Auto-rename & cleanup
set.rename.yearparens.hint: "Example Movie (2024)" instead of "Example Movie 2024". Off by default. Plex, Jellyfin and Radarr match films on the bracketed shape, so turn this on if one of those apps reads this folder
set.role.title: Recommended settings for how you use it
set.rss.dupe.hint: what happens when a new download has the same identity (show, season and episode, or title and year) as one already queued or downloaded. "Hold it paused" keeps it as a backup that starts automatically if the original fails. "Refuse it" turns the add away with an error. "Fail it into History" records it as a failed download right away, which is what Sonarr and Radarr expect so they can pick a different release themselves. Applies everywhere downloads are added, not just RSS
set.rss.dupe.pause: hold it paused as a backup
set.rss.dupescope.hint: "same show or film" treats any release with the same identity (show, season and episode, or title and year) as a duplicate, even under a different name. "same release only" matches only the same release name again, so a quality upgrade chosen by Sonarr or Radarr downloads normally while the same NZB added twice is still caught
set.rss.feeds.hint: each feed is polled on its own interval; items passing the rules are queued automatically. Rules (one per line): Require: size>200M · Require: age>2h · Reject: age>30d · Reject: *480p* · Accept: *1080p*. An Accept rule can file its matches itself: Accept(category=tv, priority=high): *1080p*. Preview shows what the rules would do without grabbing anything
set.rss.feeds.key.hint: A saved feed address is shown with its API key hidden as ***, so the box does not hold the whole address. Leave the address as it is and the saved key is kept. To change it, paste the whole new address in, key included; an address still showing *** is refused when you apply.
set.rss.title: RSS auto-grab
set.run.restart.hint: applies the settings above that need a restart. In-progress downloads stop and resume by themselves from where they got to.
set.run.stop.hint: shuts the engine down. Downloads resume where they got to when it starts again.
set.run.title: Run state
set.search.none: Nothing matches that. Try a word from the setting itself, like "quota", "folder" or "key".
set.sec.apikey.confirm: Create a new API key? The old one stops working immediately, so anything already connected (Sonarr, Radarr, NZB360) has to be given the new key.
set.sec.apikey.copied: API key copied to the clipboard.
set.sec.apikey.hint: Sonarr, Radarr, NZB360 and anything else that connects to nzbfast needs this. Show it to copy it across, or create a new one (then paste the new one into those apps). Typing your own here replaces it; leaving it blank keeps the current one
set.sec.apikey.new.ok: New API key created. Paste it into Sonarr, Radarr or anything else that connects to nzbfast.
set.sec.apikey.newcopied: New API key created and copied. Paste it into Sonarr, Radarr or anything else that connects to nzbfast.
set.sec.apikey.none: No key is set: this daemon is open to anyone who can reach it.
set.sec.apikey.shown: API key shown - copy it from the box.
set.sec.backup.confirm: Restore this backup? Every setting, server and key on this install is replaced by what the backup holds, and nzbfast restarts to apply it.
set.sec.backup.done: Backup downloaded. It holds passwords and keys - keep the file private.
set.sec.backup.hint: one file holding every setting, your servers (passwords included) and both keys - keep it somewhere private. Restoring it on a fresh install brings everything back
set.sec.backup.notone: That file is not an nzbfast backup.
set.sec.backup.restored: Backup restored - restarting nzbfast to apply it.
set.sec.backup.winrestart: Restored. Restart nzbfast from the system tray to apply it.
set.sec.bind.hint: which address the dashboard and API answer on. 0.0.0.0 is the default and answers on every network this machine is on, which is what a NAS, a container or any headless box needs. 127.0.0.1 answers on this machine only, so nothing else on your network can reach it even with the key - pair that with a reverse proxy or a VPN. Careful: an address this machine does not have stops the next start from coming up at all, and the only way back is to fix it in settings.json by hand
set.sec.cors.hint: which web pages a browser will let read this API. * is the default and matches SABnzbd, so extensions like NZB Unity and NZBDonkey work with no setup - your API key is still needed on every request. To keep it tighter, list the origins you allow instead (https://example.com), separated by commas. Empty sends no header at all, which blocks every extension
set.sec.nzbkey.confirm: Create a new NZB key? The old one stops working immediately, so anything already submitting NZBs with it (NZB Donkey, scripts) has to be given the new key.
set.sec.nzbkey.copied: NZB key copied to the clipboard.
set.sec.nzbkey.hint: add-only key: may submit NZBs and pass connection tests, but not see or change anything else
set.sec.nzbkey.new.ok: New NZB key created. Paste it into anything that submits NZBs with the add-only key.
set.sec.nzbkey.newcopied: New NZB key created and copied. Paste it into anything that submits NZBs with the add-only key.
set.sec.nzbkey.none: No NZB key is set. Create one, or type your own in the box.
set.sec.nzbkey.shown: NZB key shown - copy it from the box.
set.sec.open.title: No API key is set, so every device on your network - and any web page you visit, via CSRF - can control this daemon. Type a key below to require auth.
set.sec.title: Security
set.sec.tlscert.hint: serve the dashboard and API over HTTPS: point this at a PEM certificate file (a chain works too) and the row below at its private key, then restart. Leave both empty for plain HTTP. A reverse proxy or a VPN like Tailscale also works and needs nothing here - the manual's security section compares the options
set.sec.tlskey.hint: the PEM private key that belongs to the certificate above. With both rows set, the next restart answers on https instead of http
set.skipsample.hint: do not download sample and proof clips at all, so you never pay for a teaser you were only going to delete. A file counts as a sample only if its name says so and it is a small slice of the release, so a full-length film whose title happens to contain the word, and a job whose only video is sample-named, are always fetched in full. A skipped file is treated as deliberately absent: repair leaves it alone and the job still completes normally. Off by default, because before the bytes arrive the name is the only evidence there is and a skip cannot be undone. Leaving it off costs a teaser's worth of bandwidth, and "Remove junk files" below already deletes samples once the download has finished. Samples packed inside the archive are not affected either way
set.smart.rules.hint: each added NZB's name runs through these top to bottom: first match wins. Match/but-not are regexes or wildcards like *anime* (plain keywords work too); sizes like 200M, 4G; category picks the subfolder of the download root. TV = when the job finishes, file it as [Show]/Season NN/ and rename the video to "Show - S01E02"
set.smart.title: Smart folders
set.snd.blurb: All synthesized right here in the browser: no audio files, nothing stored on the server. Preferences are per-browser.
set.snd.events.hint: uncheck any you don't want · ▶ plays a preview (works even with the master switch off)
set.snd.master.hint: master switch for everything below, including the button-press blip
set.snd.popup.hint: a refused or failed action also raises a desktop notification, so you see it when this page is behind something else. Errors only - everything else stays in the page
set.snd.saylen.short: short name: stop before the year/quality
set.snd.saylen.title: how much of a release name to speak
set.snd.speed.hint: ticks: a geiger-style click every N MB downloaded, so a faster line ticks faster (N defaults to about one tick per second at your current speed) · tone: a soft pip every few seconds whose pitch rises and falls with the download rate
set.snd.title: Sounds
set.snd.tts.hint: speak events aloud, naming the file ("Download complete: …") with your browser's built-in voices; nothing leaves this machine · choose which events talk with the 🗣 boxes below
set.snd.voice.hint: the voice list comes from your browser and OS; more can usually be installed in system settings
set.speed.adaptive.hint: a connection that goes quiet is cut in seconds instead of half a minute, judged against that server's usual response time; a slow but alive transfer is never cut. In fault tests it cleared dead-air stalls about 4x sooner, helped further when a whole server went mute, and dropped nothing on a spiky but healthy link
set.speed.auto.hint: RTT-governed: yields to other household traffic, under the cap
set.speed.autoconn.hint: while idle, measure each provider's connection sweet spot and cap downloads at it: asking a provider for too many sockets can be several times SLOWER than the right number. Set a Line speed below and every result is also scored against it, so you can see how close your providers get and what is worth changing
set.speed.defer.hint: a job stuck on one slow server while others wait is sent to the back of the queue (progress kept; it resumes when the queue is clear)
set.speed.line.bits: Your measured peak is about an eighth of this Line speed. Providers quote megabits: if your line is 1 Gbps, enter 1Gbps, not 1G or 1GB.
set.speed.line.hint: your connection's full speed. Units matter and both are accepted: 900Mbps or 1Gbps for the number your provider quotes (they sell megabits), 112MB/s or a bare 112M for megabytes. This is the yardstick connection tuning is scored against - every ladder says how close it got, and the note below says what to do about a gap. Tuning never stops measuring at this number, so a line faster than the setting still reads true and is reported back to you. Also lets remote apps set percentage speed limits, SABnzbd-style
set.speed.oracleroute: Providers the oracle says are gone go last
set.speed.oracleroute.hint: experimental: when the availability check is confident a provider's backbone has lost a release (takedown), that provider is asked LAST for that download instead of first. It only changes the ORDER: nothing is removed, so a written-off provider is still asked once every other server has missed the article, and a wrong call costs a little time rather than the download. Off by default
set.speed.oraclesample.hint: while nothing is downloading, ask each server about a few articles of indexed releases and remember the answers: that is the picture the setting above reads, and what lets a dead post be recognised before you queue it. Counted per server per hour; 0 turns the checking off. Default 300. Needs the built-in indexer, and stands down entirely while a download runs
set.speed.posthealth.hint: while nothing is downloading, ask every server about a few of each queued post's articles and mark the row with the answer: a post your providers no longer carry is worth knowing about before the bandwidth is spent, not at 97%. Costs a few dozen tiny requests per job, plus a short read of the post's repair data, which is skipped on a prepaid block account. A clean result means the articles answered, not that their contents are intact: a small number of providers answer for removed articles with dummy data, which only the real download catches
set.speed.posthealthdefer.hint: a job whose check came back bad waits behind items of the same priority that checked out better. It only changes the ORDER: nothing is removed, paused or failed, and forcing a job or raising its priority overrides it. On by default: a post uploaded moments ago can look missing everywhere too, but it only waits behind healthier items and still downloads
set.speed.posthealthfail: Give up on posts no server can supply
set.speed.posthealthfail.hint: a job fails without downloading when EVERY one of your servers said EVERY sampled article was missing and the post is too old for that to be propagation. Sonarr or Radarr then blocklists the release and looks for another one straight away, instead of waiting out a download that cannot finish. Off by default and deliberately hard to trigger: one silent server, or one article still present, and the job runs as normal. Even so, a provider having a bad five minutes can look exactly like a dead post, so turn this on only if you would rather lose the occasional good release than spend the bandwidth. Needs the check above
set.speed.prefetch.hint: servers the active download can't use (its articles aren't on them) start the next queued job instead of idling; off automatically when a quota is set
set.speed.race.hint: near the end of a download, idle connections fetch the last slow articles a second time and the first copy wins; a connection running far below its siblings is reconnected. Finishes jobs sooner for a fraction of a percent of extra traffic
set.speed.sched.hint: rules fire in this machine's local time; on (re)start the most recent rule at-or-before now wins
set.speed.title: Speed & scheduling
set.speed.updchecks.hint: show a notice when a new version is published: nzbfast never downloads or installs updates by itself; off = never check at all
set.speed.updurl.hint: release manifest the daemon polls every 6 h; empty disables checking
set.spot.adult: Roughly a third of spots are filed as adult by the people who posted them. Those are left out of Browse unless you tick Include adult there.
set.spot.backfill.hint: how far back to read on the first pass. Later passes carry on from where the last one stopped, so this is paid once
set.spot.cant: What it is not: a replacement for an indexer account. Spots only cover what somebody chose to announce, which is a fraction of what gets posted.
set.spot.deepen.hint: articles of older Spotnet history to read each pass, on top of the new ones. The feed goes back to 2011 and the walk stops by itself once it reaches the start, so this is temporary work with a lasting result. 0 turns it off
set.spot.enabled.hint: on by default. Spotnet is a public feed where people announce what they have posted and sign it with their own key. Each spot carries the real title and the NZB, so it names releases a header scan cannot see. It works with the built-in indexer off.
set.spot.groups.hint: comma-separated. free.pt is the one active Spotnet group; there is rarely a reason to change this
set.spot.resolve.hint: opening a spot fetches the NZB behind it and turns it into a card, so this is the part that costs traffic. Newest spots go first, so a deep backlog never holds up today's. 0 turns it off
set.spot.title: Spotnet spots
set.spot.what: What it finds: around 170 to 200 new spots a day. Most are Dutch or Belgian, with a steady minority of English scene releases. Every spot is checked against the signature of the person who posted it before it is stored, and one that does not check out is thrown away.
set.spot.where: Spots land on the wall as named cards next to everything else you index, each carrying a spot badge so it is always clear where the name came from. Browse also keeps a raw Spots list, which is where adult spots stay unless you ask for them. Downloading one fetches the NZB it points at and queues it like any other download.
set.srv.bindip.hint: the local IP address this server's connections leave from, for a machine with more than one internet link (two lines on a router, or a VPN alongside the normal one). Blank lets the system choose. The kind of address decides the kind it reaches: an IPv4 address here connects to the server over IPv4
set.srv.block.hint: for an account where you paid up front for a fixed amount of data: nzbfast counts what it has used and stops using this server when that data is gone. 0 = an unlimited plan. Give it a tier of 1 or more so it only fills in what your main servers missed
set.srv.blockref.confirm: Restart the used counter for {host} at zero? Do this after buying a new block - the usage history is kept.
set.srv.blockref.hint: when you top up this account, press the button to restart the used counter at zero. The usage history is kept
set.srv.capped: capped at {g} on {n} of the last {d} days
set.srv.capped.nolo: capped on {n} of the last {d} days
set.srv.capped.title: on these days this provider refused another connection while it was already serving {g}, out of the {m} set here. Nothing is wrong with the account. If it does not match what you pay for, this is the record to send them.
set.srv.capped.title.nolo: on these days this provider refused another connection while it was already serving fewer than the {m} set here. These days were recorded before nzbfast kept the figure for each one, so how many it allowed is not known for them. Nothing is wrong with the account. If it does not match what you pay for, this is the record to send them.
set.srv.capset: capped at {n} by the Connections setting
set.srv.capset.title: downloads use at most {n} connections per server, from the Connections setting in Settings; this account allows {m}. Raise Connections to use more of its allowance.
set.srv.carry.busy: Not tested: a download is running. This test opens its own connections, so running it now would take capacity from the job. Unpacking and repair count as running too - try again when nothing is left in the queue.
set.srv.carry.capped: It will not go above {max} on its own. To go higher, set "Total connections across all servers" in Settings to the number you want - the new number applies from the next download, with no restart. To lift it for this server alone, turn on "Use exactly this many" in this editor.
set.srv.carry.flat: Twice as many connections carried no more in total, so your line or the route to this server is already full and extra connections would not help.
set.srv.carry.fleet: At that speed your line would want about {want} connections in total to fill it. nzbfast is using {now}.
set.srv.carry.hint: how fast ONE connection to this server actually runs, measured rather than assumed. It matters because nzbfast decides how many connections to open by dividing your line speed by what it expects each one to carry, and on some routes - a provider on the other side of the world is the usual one - each connection runs far slower than that, so the number it opens is too small and your line sits half empty. Measuring costs a little of your allowance and opens real connections for a few seconds, so it only ever runs when you press this. Nothing is changed by it: it tells you what it found
set.srv.carry.live: Your last download's connections carried about {live} each at their best, counting every server together. This test measured {host} on its own.
set.srv.carry.none: This server accepted no connections at all, so there was nothing to measure. That usually means the account is already in use somewhere else, or your plan allows fewer connections than the box above asks for.
set.srv.carry.onerung: Whether more connections would help could not be tested, because this account allows too few connections to compare two sizes.
set.srv.carry.partly: Twice as many connections carried somewhat more, so there is a little left to gain here but not a lot.
set.srv.carry.running: Measuring - this takes about a quarter of a minute.
set.srv.carry.scales: Twice as many connections carried twice as much, so more connections here would go faster.
set.srv.certname.hint: only for a server whose security certificate is issued to a different name from the one you connect to. That happens when you reach a server of your own by its address or its name on your own network, or when a provider sits behind another company's front end. Put the name the certificate was issued to here and connect to whatever you like: the certificate is still checked in full, and still has to be issued by a recognised authority - all this changes is which name it has to be issued to. Blank, which is right for almost everyone, checks the name or address you connect to. It takes a name, never an address
set.srv.comp.title: of all articles requested from this server over its lifetime, how many it actually had
set.srv.disable.title: Take this server out of the pool without removing it
set.srv.enable.title: Put this server back in the pool
set.srv.family.hint: which kind of internet address to try first, when this server has both an IPv4 and an IPv6 one. Automatic tries IPv4 first, which suits almost everyone. Pick IPv6 first if your home network reaches IPv4 only through your internet provider's translator, where IPv6 is the quicker path. Whichever you pick, the other kind is still tried if the first does not answer. One caution on macOS: it makes itself fresh IPv6 addresses for privacy every so often, so a usenet provider that counts how many places use your account at once can read one machine as several. If yours limits that, set a bind address below as well, to a fixed IPv6 address of this machine
set.srv.fills.title: only queried for articles the primaries could not find: filling those gaps is its whole job, so a lower number here is expected
set.srv.group.hint: servers you give the same name here are treated as one source: many brands resell the same network (optional)
set.srv.group.sug: looks like the {name} network: brands on one network answer alike
set.srv.group.sug.same: same network as {host}: brands on one network answer alike
set.srv.idlekeep.hint: how many connections survive that hang-up, so the next download still starts warm. Blank = choose for me. On a provider that limits ADDRESSES this makes no difference: this machine is one address whether it holds one connection or sixty, so keeping any at all leaves the account occupied and the sensible answer there is none
set.srv.idlerel.capwarn: this account limits addresses, so keeping any will not free it for your other machines
set.srv.idlerel.hint: seconds with nothing downloading before nzbfast closes this server's connections, freeing the account for your other machines. The next download opens fresh ones, which costs a moment at the start. Blank = choose for me, based on the address limit above. 0 = never hang up, which is right when this machine is the only thing using the account
set.srv.import.title: Scan this machine for SABnzbd / NZBGet configs and import their servers
set.srv.ips.hint: how many places may use this account at the same time, from your provider's plan. Not the same as connections above: that is how many connections ONE machine opens, this is how many machines, sites or homes may connect at all. Leave blank if you do not know and nzbfast will use a safe guess
set.srv.ips.wan.b: More than one internet connection? If this machine reaches the internet over several links (a router balancing two lines, or a multi-WAN setup), each connection can go out from a different address and use up several slots at once. Set a bind address on this server to pin it to one link.
set.srv.ips.where.b: Sign in to your provider's own website (the member area, control panel or "my account" page) and open the page for your plan or subscription. Look for wording like IP addresses, locations, devices or simultaneous logins. It is often printed next to the connection count and is a much smaller number: 1, 2 or 3 is common, and many providers set no limit at all. Your welcome email may say it too. If nothing mentions one, leave this blank.
set.srv.ips.why.b: Why it matters. Holding a connection open makes the next download start faster, but it also keeps one of these address slots occupied while nothing is downloading. If you run nzbfast somewhere else too, or use this account from a laptop, a seedbox or another home, an idle machine can quietly lock the others out. With a limit of 1 or 2 that happens straight away. nzbfast uses this number to decide how soon to hang up when idle.
set.srv.level.hint: 0 = primary; a level-N server only fetches articles every lower level missed: fill/backup economics
set.srv.none: no servers configured: add your provider below
set.srv.paid.chip.title: every byte from this server is billed, so nzbfast never sends it traffic of its own: no automatic connection tests, no benchmark traffic, no header scans
set.srv.paid.hint: turn this on for a metered account, where you pay for what you download. Your files still come from this server exactly as before; what stops is nzbfast spending bytes here for its own benefit, such as automatic connection tests, benchmark traffic and header scans for the index. Leave it off for an unlimited plan
set.srv.paid.sug: fill tiers are usually paid blocks: turn this on if you pay for this server by the byte
set.srv.pin.hint: auto-tuning still measures this server and still reports what it found, but the number above wins. Turn this on when you have timed real downloads yourself and the tuner disagrees with you
set.srv.ret.hint: 0 = unlimited; older articles route to deeper servers
set.srv.samebb: {hosts} look like the same network under different brands ({bb}). When one of them is missing an article, the others almost never have it, so they do not back each other up.
set.srv.samebb.cover: For real coverage, add a server on a different backbone: a subscription or a small block account both work.
set.srv.samebb.group: If that is what you want, give them the same Provider network name so they are treated as one source.
